items.title: TT_METAL_WATCHER segfaults in open_mesh_device on Wormhole T3K (1x8) — models unit CI job cannot run on this board
items.body:
### Summary

`TT_METAL_WATCHER=30` hard-segfaults during `open_mesh_device` on a Wormhole T3K
(1x8, 4x n300). The **models unit CI job sets this variable**, so the unit suite as
configured cannot run on this board. With the watcher disabled the same suite
completes normally.

This is not gemma4-specific — the crash is in mesh open / Fabric init, before any
model code runs. Flagging it because a segfault at this point is easy to
misattribute to whatever model happens to be under test.

### Repro

```bash
export TT_METAL_WATCHER=30
HF_MODEL=models/demos/gemma4/configs/gemma-4-E2B-it \
  pytest models/demos/gemma4/tests/unit/    # any device test on 1x8
```

### Observed

```
Watcher server initialized, disabled features: None (watcher_server.cpp:568)
Watcher checking device 0..7 (watcher_device_reader.cpp:422)
Initializing Fabric (fabric_firmware_initializer.cpp:308)
Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault
  File ".../ttnn/ttnn/distributed/distributed.py", line 671 in open_mesh_device
```

The same invocation with the watcher unset completes: `270 passed, 3 failed, 89 skipped`
(the 3 were unrelated missing PCC gates, since fixed).

A second suite in the same session aborted at the same point with SIGABRT rather
than SIGSEGV, so the failure mode is not perfectly deterministic — but the crash
site (`open_mesh_device`, during Fabric init, with watcher enabled) was identical.

### Impact

The models unit job exports `TT_METAL_WATCHER=30`. On this WH board that job
cannot start, independent of model. Anyone enabling watcher on Wormhole 1x8 will
hit it.

### Environment

- Board: Wormhole T3K, 1x8 (4x n300, 8 ASICs)
- tt-metal: `arg/gemma4_1x8optiom` @ 4738b357c48 (clean build, submodules synced)
- Workaround: unset `TT_METAL_WATCHER`

items.title: [Bug] Metal 2.0 spec validation uses a default-constructed DispatchCoreConfig, rejecting valid placements on ETH-dispatch devices
items.body:
## Summary

`ValidateNodeBounds` derives the compute worker grid from a default-constructed `DispatchCoreConfig{}` (WORKER dispatch) instead of the device's actual dispatch core config. On an ETH-dispatch device the two disagree, and validation rejects
placements that placement itself produced:

```
TT_FATAL: WorkUnitSpec 'main' targets node (0,7), which is out of bounds.
The compute worker grid on this device is 8x7.
```

| | API used | ETH-dispatch mock |
|---|---|---|
| Placement | `device->compute_with_storage_grid_size()` | **8x8** - `(0,7)` is a worker |
| Validation | `ValidateNodeBounds` with default `DispatchCoreConfig{}` | **8x7** - `(0,7)` rejected |

So an op factory legitimately targets `(0,7)`, then validation fails it.

## Where

`tt_metal/impl/metal2_host_api/program_spec.cpp:625`, in `ValidateNodeBounds`.
The real-device path reads the actual config; the mock path keeps the default:

```cpp
DispatchCoreConfig dispatch_core_config{};   // default => WORKER
uint8_t num_hw_cqs = 1;

// But, best get the real dispatch_core_config and num_hw_cqs
// (Makes no difference now, but hardbaking that assumption could be brittle)
if (!is_mock) {
    auto& dispatch_mgr = MetalContext::instance().get_dispatch_core_manager();
    dispatch_core_config = dispatch_mgr.get_dispatch_core_config();
    num_hw_cqs = dispatch_mgr.get_num_hw_cqs();
}
```

The existing comment anticipates this: it does make a difference once the mock is ETH-dispatch. Note `ValidateNodeBounds(const ProgramSpec&)` takes only the spec, so a caller has no way to supply the correct config.

## Why the mock path is reached at all

tt-mlir's OpModel clears the program cache before every constraint query, so
every query takes the cache-miss path and hits `ValidateNodeBounds`.

## Trigger: not yet identified

The mismatch above is the *mechanism* that makes this fatal, but it is not the
trigger. `ValidateNodeBounds` is byte-identical between a known-good pin and a
known-bad one, so something else began targeting row 7:

| metal pin | `MockAllocatorViewTripwireTest.PadViewReportsL1Address0` |
|---|---|
| `d5f9bc4a43b1287523458f1af6a470c6b2adc180` | passes (872 ms — query returns an address) |
| `58342a6f63d822599484977d61dcd8f3993350f0` | `TT_FATAL` above (9 ms — dies in validation) |

Known-good is `d5f9bc4a`, not the `d7f3415767d65cb98a0f23ae6a450191a7aff606`
recorded on tenstorrent/tt-mlir#9235. Both pins already contain #53084
(`ab553c4`, which re-enabled miss-path validation), so #53084 is **not** the
cause of this particular failure. Something in the 229-commit range
`d5f9bc4a..58342a6f` changed either the mock's compute grid or `ttnn.pad`'s
placement. Bisect in progress; will update with the commit.

Either way the default-constructed config is worth fixing on its own: it makes
any such change fail as an out-of-bounds abort rather than a usable result.

## Expected

Validation should read the device's dispatch core config rather than default-constructing one, so placement and validation agree on the grid.

## Impact on tt-mlir

Tracked as https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-mlir/issues/9235. OpModel constraint queries on mock devices fail rather than returning constraints. Currently mitigated by returning a failed query instead of crashing, which forced skipping `MockAllocatorViewTripwireTest.PadViewReportsL1Address0`. Both the workaround and the skip should be removed once this is fixed.

## Repro

`TTMLIR_ENABLE_OPMODEL=ON`, any OpModel constraint query on a mock device whose
dispatch config is not the default, against an op whose factory targets row 7.

Concretely, at metal `58342a6f`: `MockAllocatorViewTripwireTest.PadViewReportsL1Address0`
in `test/unittests/Optimizer/TestL1SpillManagementMockAllocator.cpp` (`ttnn.pad`,
n150 mock). The same abort is reported on an 8-chip mock (`t3k_cluster_desc.yaml`)
for `ttnn.typecast` / `ttnn.permute` / `ttnn.repeat` in tenstorrent/tt-mlir#9235.

items.title: ttnn.ge / ttnn.le (tensor-scalar): ge/le are lane-wise complements of lt/gt, so they cannot match IEEE NaN semantics, and heaviside cannot emit NaN at all - the tensor-tensor kernels (2026) already carry the explicit NaN rejection
items.body:
**Component / Area:** kernels

The tensor-scalar comparison kernels still carry their original 2023 form. The tensor-tensor comparison kernels were rewritten in 2026 with explicit NaN rejection that the scalar kernels never received. The same public op therefore runs two different kernels depending on the overload, and only one of them can be NaN-correct:

- The scalar overload `ge(Tensor, float)` reaches `calculate_unary_ge` (`ckernel_sfpu_unary_comp.h`, 2023) via `ttnn::ge_unary` and `unary_ge_tile`: [`binary.cpp:491`](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/ttnn/cpp/ttnn/operations/eltwise/binary/binary.cpp#L491), [`unary.cpp:274`](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/ttnn/cpp/ttnn/operations/eltwise/unary/unary.cpp#L274), [`comp.h:198-200`](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tt_metal/hw/inc/api/compute/eltwise_unary/comp.h#L198-L200)
- The tensor overload `ge(Tensor, Tensor)` reaches `calculate_binary_comp_fp32_weak_ordered` (`ckernel_sfpu_binary_comp.h`, 2026) through binary_ng

The scalar comparison kernels are byte-identical on Wormhole and Blackhole, and heaviside's branch logic is identical on both.

### The core defect needs no hardware to prove

`calculate_unary_ge` and `calculate_unary_lt` evaluate the same predicate and return opposite constants ([`ckernel_sfpu_unary_comp.h:99-134`](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tt_metal/hw/ckernels/wormhole_b0/metal/llk_api/llk_sfpu/ckernel_sfpu_unary_comp.h#L99-L134)):

```c
// lt:                          // ge:
v_if(v < s) { v = 1.0f; }       v_if(v < s) { v = 0.0f; }
v_else      { v = 0.0f; }       v_else      { v = 1.0f; }
```

So `ge(x, s) == 1.0 - lt(x, s)` holds on every lane by construction, and likewise `le(x, s) == 1.0 - gt(x, s)`. The reference (IEEE 754, torch) requires every ordered comparison with NaN to be false: `torch.lt`, `le`, `gt`, `ge` all return False on NaN; only `ne` returns True. Two ops defined as complements of each other cannot both return 0.0 on a NaN lane. Whatever truth value the SFPU assigns to `NaN < s`, exactly one member of each pair diverges from torch. That claim is independent of the hardware's compare behavior.

### Expected direction, stated as contingent

Two artifacts in the tree indicate the SFPU float predicate cannot see NaN: #52036 (the xlogy guard `in1 == nan` can never be true), and [`ckernel_sfpu_comp.h:108-150`](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tt_metal/hw/ckernels/wormhole_b0/metal/llk_api/llk_sfpu/ckernel_sfpu_comp.h#L108-L150), where the `*z` comparison kernels detect NaN with integer `|v| > inf` chains precisely because the float predicate does not. Under that behavior (`NaN < s` evaluates false), the expected outputs for a float32 NaN lane against s = 1.0 are:

| op | scalar overload (expected) | tensor overload | torch |
|---|---|---|---|
| gt, lt, eq | 0.0 | 0.0 | 0.0 (False) |
| **ge** | **1.0** | 0.0 | 0.0 |
| **le** | **1.0** | 0.0 | 0.0 |

giving `ge(NaN) = 1.0` while `gt(NaN) = 0.0` and `eq(NaN) = 0.0`, so within the scalar API alone, ge disagrees with (gt OR eq). A NaN *scalar* would make the entire output constant 1.0 for the same reason. I have not run this on hardware: the direction column is what the two artifacts above predict, and one run of the repro below confirms or flips it. The complement argument in the previous section does not depend on which way it lands.

### Same mechanism, second op: heaviside cannot emit NaN on any path

[`ckernel_sfpu_heaviside.h:28-31`](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tt_metal/hw/ckernels/wormhole_b0/metal/llk_api/llk_sfpu/ckernel_sfpu_heaviside.h#L28-L31):

```c
v_if(v < 0.0f) { v = 0.0f; }
v_elseif(v > 0.0f) { v = 1.0f; }
v_else { v = s; }
```

The output set is exactly {0.0, 1.0, value}; no path forwards the input. `torch.heaviside(NaN, v)` returns NaN. This finding is unconditional: whichever branch a NaN lane lands in (the v_else under unordered-false, the v > 0 branch if the compare is sign-bit based), the kernel manufactures a definite value from NaN, so `ttnn.heaviside(NaN, 5.0)` returns 5.0 or 1.0, never NaN.

### The fix already exists in the tree

`ckernel_sfpu_binary_comp.h` rejects NaN in every comparison family: eq/ne at [lines 62-63](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tt_metal/hw/ckernels/wormhole_b0/metal/llk_api/llk_sfpu/ckernel_sfpu_binary_comp.h#L62-L63), lt/gt at [104-105](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tt_metal/hw/ckernels/wormhole_b0/metal/llk_api/llk_sfpu/ckernel_sfpu_binary_comp.h#L104-L105), le/ge at [158-160](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tt_metal/hw/ckernels/wormhole_b0/metal/llk_api/llk_sfpu/ckernel_sfpu_binary_comp.h#L158-L160), where the weak-ordered kernel stores 0 when `abs(a) + abs(b) > inf`. The `*z` unary kernels in `ckernel_sfpu_comp.h` carry the same chains. The tensor-scalar comparisons and heaviside are the only members of the family without it. This is the same 2023-unary versus 2026-binary split documented for fmod/remainder in #51441.

### Repro (needs hardware; float32, not bfloat16)

```python
import torch, ttnn
dev = ttnn.open_device(device_id=0)
x = torch.full((32, 32), float("nan"), dtype=torch.float32)
t = ttnn.from_torch(x, dtype=ttnn.float32, layout=ttnn.TILE_LAYOUT, device=dev)

ttnn.to_torch(ttnn.ge(t, 1.0))                  # scalar overload -> 2023 kernel; expected 1.0
ttnn.to_torch(ttnn.ge(t, ttnn.ones_like(t)))    # tensor overload -> 2026 kernel; expected 0.0
ttnn.to_torch(ttnn.gt(t, 1.0))                  # expected 0.0; ge != (gt or eq) if the row above is 1.0
ttnn.to_torch(ttnn.heaviside(t, 5.0))           # expected 5.0; torch gives NaN
torch.ge(x, 1.0)                                 # reference: all False
```

bfloat16 cannot carry the probe: host-side packing collapses NaN to +inf before the SFPU sees it ([`ckernel_sfpu_exp2.h:76-79`](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/main/tt_metal/hw/ckernels/wormhole_b0/metal/llk_api/llk_sfpu/ckernel_sfpu_exp2.h#L76-L79)), and the tensor then legitimately compares as inf.

Refs #52036, #52930, #51557, #51441.

items.title: [runtime]: Scope tensor prefetcher trace state by sub-device manager
items.body:
## Issue Metadata

**Component / Area:** Runtime / Tensor prefetcher / mesh trace lifecycle

**Issue Type:** Other

## Issue Description

### Observed

`MeshTraceId` has always been scoped to a given `SubDeviceManagerId`; PR #53735 documents this existing contract more clearly. The Tensor prefetcher does not currently preserve that scope:

- [`trace_requests_`](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/669e6869b53188f992f6a53d1774434ba716fe2a/tt_metal/impl/buffers/tensor_prefetcher_manager.hpp#L212) is keyed only by `MeshTraceId`.
- [Capture](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/669e6869b53188f992f6a53d1774434ba716fe2a/tt_metal/impl/buffers/tensor_prefetcher_manager.cpp#L998) appends requests to that unscoped numeric bucket.
- [Replay](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/669e6869b53188f992f6a53d1774434ba716fe2a/tt_metal/impl/buffers/tensor_prefetcher_manager.cpp#L1013) and [release](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/669e6869b53188f992f6a53d1774434ba716fe2a/tt_metal/impl/buffers/tensor_prefetcher_manager.cpp#L1132) look up or erase the same unscoped key.

When a caller explicitly reuses custom trace ID `x` under managers A and B, both captures land in the same prefetcher bucket. Replaying either trace queues both sets of captured requests, and releasing either trace removes the captured requests belonging to the other manager.

This only affects explicit/custom trace IDs. Default-generated trace IDs are globally unique, so they do not collide across managers.

Originally identified in the [Codex review comment on #53735](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/pull/53735#issuecomment-5426538995).

#### Evidence for manager-scoped interpretation

The existing mesh-trace lifecycle does not resolve a `MeshTraceId` against a device-global trace table:

- Each [`SubDeviceManager` instance owns its own `trace_buffer_pool_`](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/a6c0acfae421813dabba60b84b002adc2a0e2016/tt_metal/impl/sub_device/sub_device_manager.hpp#L108), which is an `unordered_map` keyed by `MeshTraceId`. Its [create, get, and release operations](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/a6c0acfae421813dabba60b84b002adc2a0e2016/tt_metal/impl/sub_device/sub_device_manager.cpp#L137-L151) operate only on that manager-local map.
- [`begin_mesh_trace`](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/a6c0acfae421813dabba60b84b002adc2a0e2016/tt_metal/distributed/mesh_device.cpp#L1414-L1423) first obtains the active `SubDeviceManager`, checks the ID only in that manager, and creates the trace in that manager's pool.
- [`end_mesh_trace`](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/a6c0acfae421813dabba60b84b002adc2a0e2016/tt_metal/distributed/mesh_device.cpp#L1439-L1445) and [`replay_mesh_trace`](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/a6c0acfae421813dabba60b84b002adc2a0e2016/tt_metal/distributed/mesh_device.cpp#L1468-L1478) likewise resolve `trace_id` through the active manager.
- [`release_mesh_trace` and `get_mesh_trace`](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/a6c0acfae421813dabba60b84b002adc2a0e2016/tt_metal/distributed/mesh_device.cpp#L1374-L1392) also dispatch to the active manager before erasing or looking up the ID. The tracker defines the current manager ID as the [ID of that active manager](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/a6c0acfae421813dabba60b84b002adc2a0e2016/tt_metal/impl/sub_device/sub_device_manager_tracker.cpp#L142-L157).

Therefore a numeric `MeshTraceId` is interpreted in the context of the current `SubDeviceManagerId`; the effective identity is `(SubDeviceManagerId, MeshTraceId)`. The Tensor prefetcher breaks that model by storing requests in a single device-wide map keyed only by `MeshTraceId`.

### Expected

Tensor prefetcher trace state must use the same manager-scoped identity as the rest of the trace lifecycle. Capturing, replaying, or releasing `(manager A, x)` must not affect `(manager B, x)`.

Key captured prefetcher requests by `(SubDeviceManagerId, MeshTraceId)` and carry the active manager ID through capture, replay, and release.

## Steps to Reproduce the Issue

### 1. Steps

1. Enable/use the Tensor prefetcher on a mesh device.
2. Create two sub-device managers, A and B.
3. Load A and capture a trace containing Tensor prefetcher requests using an explicit custom trace ID `x`.
4. Load B and capture a different trace containing Tensor prefetcher requests using the same explicit custom trace ID `x`.
5. Replay either trace and observe that requests captured for both managers are queued.
6. Release either trace and observe that the captured requests for both managers are erased.

### 2. Input data / link or description

No external input is required. Use distinct prefetch request payloads under A and B so the cross-manager mixing is observable.

### 3. Frequency

Always when the same explicit/custom `MeshTraceId` is reused under different managers and both traces capture Tensor prefetcher requests. Not reproducible through the default trace-ID allocation path because those IDs are globally unique.

## System Details

**Software Versions:** Observed while reviewing PR #53735 at commit `669e6869b53188f992f6a53d1774434ba716fe2a`.

**Hardware Details:** Hardware-independent bookkeeping issue; any configuration that exercises the Tensor prefetcher and multiple sub-device managers should expose it.

## Regression Info

This is not a change to `MeshTraceId` semantics: manager scoping is the longstanding behavior. The contract was previously under-documented and is made explicit by PR #53735.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Captured Tensor prefetcher requests are keyed by `(SubDeviceManagerId, MeshTraceId)`.
- Capture, replay, and release all use the active manager ID.
- A regression test reuses the same custom trace ID under two managers and verifies independent replay and release.
- Default-generated trace IDs continue to work unchanged.

items.title: [Bug] ttnn.pow_bw returns +inf for every negative base, where the gradient is finite
items.body:
**Component / Area:** ttnn eltwise binary_backward

**Issue Type:** Bad Outputs

## Observed

`pow_bw(grad, a, exponent)` with `exponent = 2.0` returns `+inf` for **every negative finite base** — all 32,639 nonzero negative bfloat16 patterns, uniformly `0x7F80`, independent of magnitude. The correct gradient is `2a` (finite everywhere).

N300 and P300, `grad = 1.0`, all 65,536 bfloat16 base patterns:

| base | torch `d/da a^2` | ttnn `pow_bw` |
|---|---|---|
| 2.0 | 4.0 | 4.0 |
| -2.0 | -4.0 | **`+inf`** |
| -1.0 | -2.0 | **`+inf`** |
| any of the 32,639 negative finite patterns | `2a` | **`+inf`** |

Positive bases are exact across the sweep. Bit-identical on both architectures, so this is the composite formulation, not an SFPU quirk — consistent with a `exp(exponent * log(a))` path whose `log(negative)` NaN then collapses to `+inf` in the bf16 pack.

`exponent = 0.0` is correct (returns 0). A NaN base with finite exponent is also handled (`pow_bw(nan, 2.0)` does not diverge between the formulation and torch's NaN).

## Not established

- Whether integer-exponent special-casing is intended upstream (torch computes `2a` for exponent 2 regardless of base sign).
- float32 behavior beyond the boundary set (5/21 boundary patterns differ between the architectures only in NaN encoding).

 Full sweep artifacts: https://github.com/kinginu/tt-eager-fusion/blob/main/reports/2026-08-25-binary-backward-v0.md

## Environment

* OS: Ubuntu 22.04
* Version of software: tt-metal `04cf22f7ee` (P300), `141fbea49c5` (N300)
* Hardware: N300 and P300
